newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish debt rallies on new borrowing policy.
newsitem.headline: Swedish debt rallies on new borrowing policy.

text.p: Sweden's debt market rallied on Wednesday as the National Debt Office cut its state borrowing forecasts for the year and unveiled a new borrowing strategy it said would make Swedish bonds more competitive globally.

The Debt Office's latest forecast puts state borrowing for the year at between 20 and 30 billion Swedish crowns ($3.03 billion to $4.55 billion) down from the previous forecast of between 40 and 50 billion.
The downgrade follows a gradual increase in state income over the year, bolstered by higher tax revenue, the state's cash-in of shares in commercial bank Nordbanken and reduced net lending.
The market reaction to the news was positive with the debt market rallying and the yield curve steepening markedly, as prices fell more swiftly in long-dated maturities.
By 0900 GMT the yield on the nine-year bond had tumbled 13 basis points to 7.11 percent while the yield curve between three and nine-year bonds steepened six basis points to 176.
Sentiment was cheered further by the Debt Office's announcement of a new direction in borrowing policy.
The first effect of this was the announcement of a new 10-year benchmark bond, the 1038 series, which will mature on October 25, 1006, and have a coupon interest rate of 6.5 percent.

The office also said in a statement that it planned to issue a new five-year bond during the first half of 1997 which it may allow investors to exchange against an older short-dated issue, series 1028, which matures in January 1999.
"The debt office wants to create a better bond market and increase Sweden's competitiveness against other international markets," said Knut Hallberg, senior economist at Swedbank.
One dealer said the market's belief that the new issue would increase overseas interest in the Swedish debt market was also adding to the bullish tone.
One senior dealer said the debt office wanted to create a more even yield curve, giving investors more reinvestment opportunities.
"It is an investor friendly gesture and I can't find any weakness in it at all although some may see it as a bit market maker unfriendly perhaps," he told Reuters.

A senior economist, who asked not to be named, said the reason for the issue was to structure the Swedish bond market in line with major offshore bond markets, keeping key maturities in the two, three, five, ten and ten-year plus area.
Sweden's current seven benchmark bonds are based on four and 11 year maturities.
The economist said the debt office needed to reduce the volume on some of its existing benchmarks and spread maturities over the longer term.
Volume on the largest of the current issues, the series 1028, has soared to 135 billion crowns.
"This could give the debt office refinancing problems when the 1028 matures in January 1999," the economist told Reuters.
"If the debt office did nothing and waited for the issue to mature it would have a huge refinancing problem. It wants to smooth out the market."

In order to build up a liquid market for the new 1038 loan, the debt office is offering investors the chance to exchange holdings of loan 1028 against the new series, with an option to choose a combination of loan 1038 and cash.
This facilitates the refinancing of loan 1028 and also gives a choice to investors who do not want to lengthen the maturity of their portfolio.
